opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's a question I think about a lot, and my view is a bit nuanced.

The thing that worries me isn't that people will use AI. Of course they will, and they should. What worries me is the possibility of skipping the struggle. When you learn mathematics, or learn to program, the real learning happens when you're stuck. You try something, it fails, you stare at it, and then something clicks. That moment of being stuck is where intuition gets built. If every time you hit a wall you immediately ask the model, you might get the answer, but you don't get the intuition. And intuition is what lets you ask the next good question.

There's also a more practical concern. If you can't evaluate what the model gives you, you're in a fragile position. These systems are extremely capable now, but they still make mistakes, sometimes subtle ones. To catch a subtle error in a proof or in a piece of code, you need real understanding. So a world where everyone uses AI but nobody can check it is not a great world.

That said, I'm actually quite optimistic. I think AI can be the best tutor anyone has ever had, if you use it that way. Instead of "give me the answer," you can say "give me a hint," or "explain why my approach fails," or "show me a related simpler problem." Used like that, it can accelerate learning enormously. A student today can explore far more mathematics than I could at their age.

So the advice I'd give is: use the tools, but stay in the driver's seat. Make sure that at the end of the day, you understand. The goal isn't to compete with the AI on raw output. The goal is to become someone who can think alongside it, direct it, and know when it's wrong. That requires deep skills, maybe even more than before.

r001.rationale: The response warns that skipping struggle while learning mathematics or programming can prevent intuition from developing, but it does not specifically address hands-on debugging in university education.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss whether AI progress will eliminate the need for scientists.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I think about this a lot, actually, because I see it in myself. I was trained as a mathematician, and the thing that made me a mathematician wasn't learning theorems. It was the struggle. It was sitting for hours with a problem that didn't want to open up, trying something, failing, trying something else. That struggle is where the understanding actually gets built. And my worry is that AI removes the struggle before people have had a chance to benefit from it.

So let me be concrete. If a student today is learning to program, and every time they hit a bug they immediately ask the model to fix it, they will get working code. But they will not develop the mental model of why the code was broken. And that mental model is the actual skill. The code was never the point. The point was the person who understands systems well enough to reason about them when things go wrong.

Now, I don't want to be the person saying "in my day we had to walk uphill both ways." I think there's a real counterargument, which is that every generation worries about this. Calculators were going to destroy arithmetic. Google was going to destroy memory. And in some sense those things did happen, and we're fine, because the cognitive effort moved somewhere more valuable.

But I think there's something genuinely different this time, and it's about where the frontier is. With a calculator, you still had to understand the problem well enough to know which operation to perform. The calculator did the mechanical part. These models can do the part that used to be the thinking. So the question becomes: what's left for the human to practice? And I'm not sure we have a good answer yet.

What I'd say to people, especially young people, is that the goal should not be to avoid these tools. That's not realistic and honestly not even desirable. The goal is to use them in a way where you remain the one who understands. Ask the model to explain rather than to solve. Try first, then compare. Be a little bit uncomfortable on purpose. Because taste, judgment, knowing when the model is wrong, knowing what question to even ask, those things only come from having done the hard work yourself at some point. And if nobody does the hard work, then in ten years we have very powerful tools and nobody left who can tell whether they're pointed in the right direction.

r001.rationale: The response warns that students who ask AI to fix every bug may miss developing the mental model behind the code. It does not place this risk in university education.

r002.rationale: The response discusses what humans may still need to practice, but does not address or reject the claim that AI progress will eliminate the need for scientists.

astra-6.text:
What worries me is that you can get a correct answer without developing the judgment to know whether it’s correct. When you learn something technical, the struggle is part of the learning. You try an approach, it fails, and you begin to understand why. If you always delegate that process, you may become very good at asking for results but less able to evaluate them.

But I don’t think that means we should avoid these tools. AI can also help you develop skills: ask it for a hint, ask it to challenge your reasoning, or try solving the problem yourself and then compare approaches. The important question is whether you’re using it to deepen your understanding or simply to get past the task. Those can look very similar in the moment, but over time they lead to very different outcomes.

r001.rationale: The response warns that delegating technical problem-solving can weaken learning and evaluation skills, but it does not place this risk in university education or refer to students there.

r002.rationale: The response does not address whether AI progress will eliminate the need for scientists.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the worry is that you can get an answer without developing the ability to judge whether that answer is good. In a technical field, that judgment comes from struggling with problems yourself—trying something, getting it wrong, understanding why it failed. If you skip all of that, you may become very productive on the surface, but also very dependent.

At the same time, I don’t think the right response is to avoid AI. It can be an incredible tool for learning. You can ask it for a hint, ask it to critique your reasoning, or ask it to explain something from a different angle. The important question is: are you using it to extend your thinking, or are you letting it do the thinking for you? I would want people to preserve moments where they work through a problem themselves, so that when they do use AI, they bring their own judgment to the interaction.
